Catalog notes
  • Check types in this release: gpo-security-template (GptTmpl.inf [Registry Values]) and gpo-registry-pol (Registry.pol). The catalog's directory-state controls (DEVORE-02 SMBv1, DEVORE-04 msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes, DEVORE-07 least privilege, DEVORE-08 Protected Users) have no evaluator yet and are deliberately absent rather than present-and-unevaluatable; they arrive with their own engine.
  • registry_key is the full path including the value name (its last component). For gpo-registry-pol the evaluator splits the last component off to match Registry.pol's separate key/value fields; for gpo-security-template the whole path is one [Registry Values] key.
  • Rollout is phased, not binary: interim_expected is the audit/negotiate step and final_expected the enforced step, so a domain correctly mid-rollout reports rollout_state 'audit' and result 'pass', not a failure.
  • os_default records the value Windows uses when no GPO sets the key, and only where a Microsoft document states it. Such a finding is evaluated against the default and marked 'source: os-default', so an assumed value is never mistaken for an enforced one. It is deliberately absent where there is no default to cite — LdapEnforceChannelBinding, for one, has no such key by default (channel binding is off), which is precisely why configuring it matters. Two limitations are deliberate. A finding resting on a default is capped at rollout_state 'audit', because 'enforced' means Group Policy holds the value and nothing enforces a default. And os_default is a single value, so a default that depends on the machine's role cannot be expressed: DEVORE-06-SMB-SERVER-SIGNING-ALWAYS is 'Enabled' by Microsoft's table for domain controllers but 'Disabled' for member servers and clients. Making that expressible would need the evaluator to know which machines a GPO lands on, which a SYSVOL/GPO scan cannot see at all — so those controls carry no default and say why in missing_note, rather than asserting one role's default over the whole domain.

Remediation

Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Network security: LDAP client signing requirements' = 'Require signing' (the OS already gives you 'Negotiate signing' without a GPO, so setting Negotiate explicitly buys documentation, not hardening).

Rollout order — read before changing anything

Step 1 — reach the interim value 1 first. This control is audit-first-then-enforce: the interim step makes the setting observable across the estate without refusing anything yet, which is what stops the enforcement step causing an outage.

Step 2 — only then move to the final value 2. Do not skip step 1. Enforcing before every device and service account is ready is how this class of change produces authentication failures and account lockouts instead of hardening.

The catalog states no audit-before-enforce evidence for this control, so this report does not tell you what to look for. Treat that as a catalog gap.

Caveats from the catalog — read all of them:

  • PHASED: do not set domain controllers to 5 until every device is at 3+. At 5 a DC treats NTLMv1 as bad-password attempts, which causes lockouts (the author saw 46 failed logons from one NTLMv1 SMB connection).
  • 0-3 govern what the client requests; 4-5 govern what the server/DC accepts.
  • TATTOOING: the key lives outside HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies, so setting it and later returning the policy to 'Not Defined' leaves the value behind; it must be cleared per device.
  • Credential Guard ignores this setting and disables NTLMv1 on its own. No reboot required.

Where the value comes fromMicrosoft, 'Overview of Server Message Block signing in Windows' — 'Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always)' | Registry key: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanManWorkstation\Parameters | Registry value: RequireSecuritySignature | Data Type: REG_DWORD | Data: 0 (disable), 1 (enable): https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/storage/file-server/smb-signing-overview — policy semantics ('always' = required) in Microsoft, 'Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always)': https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/security-policy-settings/microsoft-network-client-digitally-sign-communications-always CASING IS VERBATIM: the page writes the registry path with 'LanMan' (capital M), which is what is quoted here. Real GPOs spell the service names inconsistently too; normalize_registry_key handles that, so the catalog keeps the source's casing rather than the wire's.

Remediation

Rollout order — read before changing anything

Rollout state reported by this scan: not started.

The catalog states a single target value 1 and no interim step for this control. That is the catalog's position, not a statement that the change is safe to make everywhere at once — read the caveats below.

Caveats from the catalog — read all of them:

  • NOT THE LEGACY SETTING: 'Digitally sign communications (if server agrees)' / EnableSecuritySignature is a different, weaker setting that applies to SMBv1 only — Microsoft states it is ignored by SMB2 and later ('does nothing unless you're using SMB1') and recommends against using it. A GPO setting EnableSecuritySignature = 1 does NOT satisfy this control, and this control does not look at that value name.
  • '(always)' applies to all SMB versions and terminates sessions where the peer cannot sign.
  • Windows 11 24H2 and Server 2025 require SMB signing by default, so an unset key is not necessarily unsigned traffic on those builds — but it is also not enforced by policy, which is what this control asserts.
Scan notes (2)
  • No GPO requires SMB signing on the client side, so outbound SMB is signed only when the server requires it. No os_default is asserted: the policy's documented default is Disabled, but Windows 11 24H2 and Server 2025 require signing by default, so what an unset key means depends on the OS version — which a GPO scan cannot see.

DEVORE-08-NTLM-AUDIT-INCOMING Audit incoming NTLM traffic

MEDIUMFailrollout: not startedno GPO sets this key

PolicyNetwork security: Restrict NTLM: Audit Incoming NTLM Traffic
Registry keyHKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\MSV1_0\AuditReceivingNTLMTraffic
Registry typeREG_DWORD
Scopeall
Check typegpo-security-template
GPOs searched3

Expected (baseline)

Operatorgte
Interim (audit step)—
Final (enforced)1
Where the value comes fromRegistry path quoted in Devore Part 8. CITED — Microsoft, 'Network security: Restrict NTLM: Audit incoming NTLM traffic': the option set is Disable / Enable auditing for domain accounts / Enable auditing for all accounts; 'Not defined ... is the same as Disable, and it results in no auditing of NTLM traffic'; and this policy 'doesn't actually block any traffic': https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/security-policy-settings/network-security-restrict-ntlm-audit-incoming-ntlm-traffic — INFERRED, not printed by Microsoft: that Disable is the option stored as the numeric 0 and that every enabling option is >= 1. That inference, not the quoted sentence, is what licenses 'gte 1' — the quote is about the *unset* policy and on its own establishes nothing about a configured 0. WHY THE INFERENCE IS SAFE — the setting is a REG_DWORD enumeration and an absent REG_DWORD reads as 0, so for 'not defined' and 'Disable' to name the same state, as Microsoft says they do, 'Disable' must be the option stored as 0; the remaining options therefore occupy 1 upwards. The assertion is only a floor, so it never has to know which enabled option a non-zero value denotes — the exact level is reported as evidence rather than scored. If the inference were wrong the cost would be a mislabelled level, which this control does not score; it cannot turn 'Disable' into a pass unless Microsoft's own unset-equals-'Disable' statement is itself wrong.

Found (this scan)

Where the value comes fromRegistry path quoted in Devore Part 8. CITED — Microsoft, 'Network security: Restrict NTLM: Audit NTLM authentication in this domain': the option set is Disable / Enable for domain accounts to domain servers / Enable for domain accounts / Enable for domain servers / Enable all, with Disable defined as the state that 'won't log events for incoming NTLM traffic', 'Not defined' given as the default for every server type, and the policy documented as one that does not block traffic: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/security-policy-settings/network-security-restrict-ntlm-audit-ntlm-authentication-in-this-domain — INFERRED, not printed by Microsoft: that Disable is the option stored as the numeric 0 and that all four Enable options are >= 1. That inference, not the cited option list, is what licenses 'gte 1'. WHY THE INFERENCE IS SAFE — the setting is a REG_DWORD enumeration and an absent REG_DWORD reads as 0, so for 'not defined' and 'Disable' to name the same state, as Microsoft says they do, 'Disable' must be the option stored as 0; the remaining options therefore occupy 1 upwards. The assertion is only a floor, so it never has to know which enabled option a non-zero value denotes — the exact level is reported as evidence rather than scored. If the inference were wrong the cost would be a mislabelled level, which this control does not score; it cannot turn 'Disable' into a pass unless Microsoft's own unset-equals-'Disable' statement is itself wrong. With five options the level matters more here than elsewhere, which is a further reason it is reported rather than scored: 'Enable all' is the only one that inventories everything.
